chapter: Growing up with music in Austin
title: Blues and jazz records at home; Blind Lemon Jefferson
summary: Family collected records of Bessie Smith, Mamie Smith and Louis Armstrong, and sang them note for note; he recalls Blind Lemon Jefferson.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Well, I take it there were blues singers around too, weren't there?
You know, the way I see it practically everybody around there sang the blues. But there wasn't hardly any occasion where I could name anybody, except the great piano players who played and sang.
You don't recall any of the more or less professional blues singers?
Yeah, he lived in Fort Worth. Or Dallas, somewhere like that.
Very slightly. I remember his records, though. He didn't do too much traveling, as I knew of, then.
Well, he must have been operating in the twenties -- 1923?

Yeah, around that time. See, my brothers and sisters didn't let a record come on the market that they didn't get it, that had any kind of singing, any kind of jazz in it. And especially my older sister, Nellie, she could sing just -- she could imitate Bessie Smith and Mamie Smith, and Clara --
Oh, well, this is where you were picking up --

Yeah. And I heard this all day and all night long. And that record company you'd see that dog sitting there looking at the master's voice, on the record, and I'd be sitting on the floor, just like that dog. Looking at that thing (chuckles).
And would you -- would they get records of bands, as well?
Oh, yeah, everything. Louis Armstrong. Everyone of us in our family could sing -- could hum every Louis Armstrong note. In fact, even that thing, "A Chocolate

Drop, that's me, because My Head Is Curly," and all that stuff. I like the way And on the solo, we'd sing it, everything and scat That's how it. My cousin, Duke, became like what they call the Texas offering of a Cab Calloway, you know. He had the long hair like the white man, you know. And he would do a Cab Calloway, and throw his hair all over his eyes, all those contortions.

But we -- and still in Texas, I have guys that come by, visit me, that picked up some old record of Charlie Parker's, something that was lately released or something. And the guy would come by, they all have those eight-track things in their car, and the guy will sit up there and he'll say, I want you to listen to this, and instead of listening to the record, I've got to listen to him, because they're humming right along. So they still have that thing in and around Texas. Where they've learned to sing those, or do those things note for note, just like the soloist is doing.
